# MetaVul: Agentic Harness Discovery for Vulnerability Detection

Ira Ceka, Arnav Garg, Ryan Lutz, Ting Zhang, Ratnadira Widyasari, Gail
Kaiser, Baishakhi Ray Affiliation: Columbia University Affiliation: The
Citadel Affiliation: Monash University Affiliation: University of
Victoria Affiliation: Columbia University, Department of Computer
Science Email: <iceka@cs.columbia.edu>
Email: [ag5516@columbia.edu](mailto:)
Email: [rlutz@student.citadel.edu](mailto:)
Email: <Ting.Zhang@monash.edu> Email: [ratnadiraw@uvic.ca](mailto:)
Email: <kaiser@cs.columbia.edu> Email: [rayb@cs.columbia.edu](mailto:)

###### Abstract

Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly used to automate
vulnerability detection, but reliable detection is challenging because
agents must distinguish subtle, security-relevant fixes from benign code
variation. While underlying LLM capability has improved significantly,
the accuracy of the agent still depends heavily on the _harness_: the
code that defines the scaffolding around the LLM. Harnesses are
typically fixed, and largely hand-written, limiting adaptation to
evaluator feedback. Additionally, when harnesses are static,
improvements on one dataset or model may not necessarily transfer to
others. To address these challenges, we introduce MetaVul, a
self-improving framework for harness discovery in vulnerability
detection. Starting from a seed structured reasoning scaffold, MetaVul
uses a workflow-based optimization loop to iteratively refine the
harness using feedback from paired vulnerable and patched functions, all
while preserving the structured reasoning and verdict format. At each
iteration, it searches over the full history of prior candidate
harnesses, with access to their trajectories, logs, and metrics, and it
returns a set of Pareto-optimal harnesses rather than a single best
candidate. We apply MetaVul to discover agent harnesses for
architectures including Codex CLI and Claude Code. A validation set (202
pairs) from TitanVul and CWEval is used for optimization, while the
unseen PrimeVul dataset (430 pairs) is kept as the held-out set. We
later test whether harnesses learned from one model transfer to others
not seen during optimization. Results on both frontier and small LLMs
show that the optimized harnesses improve pairwise vulnerability
detection up to 23.3 percentage points on the validation set (Opus 4.6)
and up to 25.8 points on the held-out set with a Pareto-frontier harness
(DeepSeek V4 Flash). Harnesses learned with one model also transfer to
others. We show that harnesses optimized with Opus 4.6 transfer to Opus
5, improving held-out pairwise accuracy by 14.7 points without the need
for further optimization. Code is available at
[https://github.com/ARiSE-Lab/MetaVul](https://github.com/ARiSE-Lab/MetaVul) ([ARiSE
Lab, 2026](#bib.bib2)).

## 1 Introduction

Artificial intelligence (AI) agents utilize a large language model (LLM)
as their core reasoning component for taking actions toward a given
goal. “Vibe coding,” or using AI tools, particularly by way of coding
agents, is becoming increasingly prevalent across the software industry.
Consequently, the growing volume and pace of AI-assisted code generation
increase the importance of effective vulnerability detection. LLM agents
rely not only on the capabilities of their underlying model, but also on
the harnesses that structure how those agents reason, interact with
tools, and arrive at a decision. Designing these harnesses, known as
_harness engineering_, has become a practice of its own ([Lopopolo,
2026](#bib.bib16); [Rajasekaran, 2026](#bib.bib27)). For vulnerability
detection, these harnesses are typically hand-designed and are fixed
during deployment, even though their structure and context can
substantially alter an agent’s results. In practice, vulnerability
detection is substantially affected by how the agent inspects the code,
and how the harness will shape that workflow ([Yildiz et al.,
2025](#bib.bib41)). This understanding directly motivates a harness that
can learn its design systematically through evaluation feedback.

Recent work studies the evaluation, evolution, and adaptation of agent
harnesses using graded scores, verifiers, execution traces, or prior
experience ([Lee et al., 2026](#bib.bib11); [Ursekar et al.,
2026](#bib.bib33); [Huang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib9); [Zhang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib42); [Huang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib10); [Esakkiraja
et al., 2026](#bib.bib6); [Nie et al., 2026](#bib.bib17)), while
OneDayAgent develops a fixed long-horizon harness ([Zheng et al.,
2026](#bib.bib43)); however, none investigates harness optimization for
vulnerability detection or incorporates security-specific objectives
such as CWE identification, vulnerability localization, and
vulnerable-patched discrimination. Harness engineering for vulnerability
detection, however, poses challenges.

Firstly, false alarms are costly. In practical security settings,
analysts receive far more alerts than they can effectively triage.
Several industry studies identify alert fatigue and analyst burnout as
major problems ([Tariq et al., 2025](#bib.bib30)). This problem is well
documented among traditional vulnerability-detection tools ([Charoenwet
et al., 2024](#bib.bib4); [Sajadi et al., 2026](#bib.bib28)) and
persists with recent LLM-based detectors ([Li et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib12)). As recently as April 2026, an independent security
company reported poor discriminative performance on PrimeVul ([Ding
et al., 2024](#bib.bib5))¹¹ 1 Following PrimeVul, we adopt _pairwise
accuracy_ as a core metric alongside accuracy and F1. High pairwise
accuracy indicates that the detector can distinguish vulnerable code
from its fixed version, reducing false alerts and, consequently, alert
fatigue. We explain this further in
Sec. [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Metrics ‣ 4 Experimental Design ‣ MetaVul: Agentic Harness Discovery for Vulnerability Detection").;
even Claude Opus 4.6, a flagship model shown by Anthropic to discover
previously unknown vulnerabilities [Carlini et al. (2026)](#bib.bib3),
struggled to reliably distinguish vulnerable functions from their
patched counterparts ([Walker, 2026](#bib.bib34)). These findings
further our motivation and demonstrate the outstanding and relevant
nature of vulnerability discrimination, which remains an open and
significant problem in practice. Moreover, these findings reinforce the
notion that strengthening the underlying models does not eliminate the
need for a robust design surrounding the agentic workflow. Rather,
harnesses and their associated design choices matter as they directly
affect downstream behavior.

Secondly, harness optimization is non-trivial. A vulnerability detection
harness controls how an agent inspects code, how it structures its
analysis, and how it reasons about security. Vulnerability detection as
a task, however, poses a _multi-objective_ challenge. A strong harness
not only has to accurately classify vulnerabilities, but also localize
them, identify their CWE(s), ground the conclusions in code evidence, as
well as distinguish the vulnerable functions from their patched
counterparts. [Ding et al. (2024)](#bib.bib5) show why traditional
classification metrics, such as accuracy and F1, are insufficient on
their own: models that perform well on conventional benchmarks approach
random guessing on PrimeVul’s paired evaluation. Optimizing for a single
metric may therefore reward superficial patterns rather than robust
vulnerability reasoning. HarnessDev ([Wu et al., 2026](#bib.bib39))
shows that a harness can overfit to the model that wrote it, memorize
development examples, or improve one capability while silently
regressing another. It can also overfit its search tasks: [Wang et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib35) found that, when harness evolution and evaluation
share the same tasks, the resulting improvements largely disappear on
held-out tasks, which suggests that optimization can learn task-specific
shortcuts rather than generalizable harness improvements.

Finally, defense must keep pace with AI-driven offense. With the rise of
AI-driven exploit generation, attackers are moving at immense speed. In
October 2026 alone, two critical PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed
after AI-assisted research revealed that a 14-year-old memory-safety
flaw in the PHP runtime engine allowed unauthenticated attackers to
execute malicious code remotely on servers hosting PHP-based web
applications, triggering a global security crisis ([Wiz Research,
2026](#bib.bib38)). These attacks involve auditing millions of lines of
code, mapping out reliable exploit strategies, and adapting to multiple
configurations. While offensive security is bottlenecked by compute,
defense has another challenge to tackle: to survive this offensive
scale, defenders must automate triage and blocking, but doing so can be
catastrophic due to the false positives mentioned previously. It is thus
paramount for defense to have scalable methods for identifying
suspicious code and evaluating, triaging, and applying potential fixes
quickly.

We address these challenges with MetaVul, which improves vulnerability
detection through iterative harness construction, driven by validation
feedback. The “meta” in MetaVul comes from the way MetaVul finds better
ways to find vulnerabilities, with the optimizer and detector operating
on two different levels: the optimizer designs the harness, and the
detector uses it. A sandboxed detection agent evaluates each candidate
harness during the discovery phase, and MetaVul returns a Pareto
frontier of harnesses that trade off discrimination and localization
ability. The discovered harnesses are then evaluated against held-out
datasets and unseen models, hence testing generalization. We ask whether
MetaVul improves vulnerability-detection harnesses and whether the gains
transfer to unseen data and unseen models (RQ1). We then evaluate how
MetaVul compares with other LLM-based or multi-agent vulnerability
detection methods (RQ2). Finally, we ask whether MetaVul’s gains rely on
“shortcut” exploitation, like data leakage signals, embedded answers, or
trivial verdict bias (RQ3). We find that MetaVul improves pairwise
accuracy by 11.4 to 23.3 points ($`1.6\times`$-$`4.3\times`$) on
validation and by up to 25.8 points ($`2.9\times`$) on 430 unseen
PrimeVul pairs. Harnesses also transfer to models that took no part in
optimization, with gains up to 14.7 points ($`1.7\times`$). MetaVul
outperforms prior LLM-based and multi-agent detectors and does so
without evidence of “shortcut” exploitation.

## 2 Related Work

Previous work has explored LLM-based vulnerability detection, harness
engineering and optimization, and structured reasoning strategies for
code. LLM-based vulnerability detection. [Ding et al. (2024)](#bib.bib5)
show that LLMs struggle to distinguish vulnerable functions from their
patched versions under paired evaluation. They propose pairwise accuracy
as a stricter alternative to conventional metrics, and also introduce
PrimeVul, which addresses the noisy labels and train-test duplication of
earlier datasets through stricter labeling, de-duplication, and a
chronological split. Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting ([Wei et al.,
2022](#bib.bib36)) improves pairwise performance over two-shot prompting
but stays below random guessing. GPTLens ([Hu et al., 2023](#bib.bib8))
pairs an auditor that proposes candidate vulnerabilities with a critic
that filters false positives, VulTrial ([Widyasari et al.,
2026](#bib.bib37)) makes use of courtroom-style agents that debate a
verdict, and ConfColl ([Tsai et al., 2025](#bib.bib32)) escalates from a
single agent to retrieval-augmented and multi-agent reasoning when
needed. All four methods use GPT-4o as the backbone ([OpenAI,
2024](#bib.bib18); [Tang et al., 2026](#bib.bib29)), and we compare
against them in
Sec. [6](#S6 "6 Comparison to Other Methods ‣ MetaVul: Agentic Harness Discovery for Vulnerability Detection").
Unlike GPTLens, VulTrial and ConfColl, MetaVul keeps a single detector
agent and instead optimizes its harness. At project scale, [Li et al.
(2026a)](#bib.bib12) report low recall, high false-discovery rates and
high computational cost. Harness engineering and optimization. Recent
work treats the agent harness (prompts, tools, memory, context
management and control flow) as an optimization target independent of
model weights ([Lee et al., 2026](#bib.bib11); [Ursekar et al.,
2026](#bib.bib33); [Lopopolo, 2026](#bib.bib16); [Rajasekaran,
2026](#bib.bib27)), in contrast to weight-level methods such as
ORPO ([Hong et al., 2024](#bib.bib7)). GEPA ([Agrawal et al.,
2026](#bib.bib1)) optimizes prompts from execution trajectories and
model feedback, and SecureForge ([Liu et al., 2026](#bib.bib15))
optimizes system prompts for secure code generation using automated
vulnerability auditing. Meta-Harness, MemoHarness, DarwinX, StarHarness,
and TTHE explore complementary forms of harness adaptation using
execution experience, search, held-out selection, and test-time
adaptation ([Lee et al., 2026](#bib.bib11); [Huang et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib10); [Zhang et al., 2026](#bib.bib42); [Esakkiraja
et al., 2026](#bib.bib6); [Nie et al., 2026](#bib.bib17)), and
OneDayAgent supports long-horizon execution with task decomposition,
persistent memory and output verification ([Zheng et al.,
2026](#bib.bib43)). HarnessOpt-Bench, Evo-Bench and HarnessDev evaluate
whether models can build or improve harnesses that generalize beyond
their optimization tasks ([Ursekar et al., 2026](#bib.bib33); [Huang
et al., 2026a](#bib.bib9); [Wu et al., 2026](#bib.bib39)), and [Wang
et al. (2026)](#bib.bib35) underscore the need for held-out evaluation,
showing that any apparent gains might vanish on held-out tasks, or
simply reflect that extra compute was spent searching over candidates.
Reasoning strategies for code. Structured chain-of-thought (SCoT)
organizes reasoning around program structures ([Li et al.,
2023](#bib.bib13)), Modularization-of-Thought (MoT) decomposes it into
hierarchical modules ([Pan & Zhang, 2025](#bib.bib25)), and Tree of
Thoughts (ToT) explores multiple reasoning paths ([Yao et al.,
2023](#bib.bib40)). Despite this, to our knowledge, none of these
methods have explored harness optimization for vulnerability detection,
nor tested whether such harnesses transfer to unseen datasets and
models. MetaVul automatically optimizes harnesses for this task, selects
them on security-specific objectives (telling vulnerable functions apart
from their fixes, i.e., pairwise accuracy, and joint CWE and line
localization), and evaluates them on an unseen dataset and on models
that took no part in optimization.

Figure 1: MetaVul pipeline. (1) Starting from seed $`h_{0}`$, harnesses
are discovered on the validation set. In each iteration, (1a) the
workspace stores previous harnesses and results, (1b)
$`\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{opt}}`$ proposes a new harness $`h_{t}`$, (1c)
$`\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{det}}`$ evaluates it, and (1d) the best result is
selected. The Pareto filter (1e) retains harnesses based on pairwise
accuracy and joint hit rate. Each harness is then frozen and tested on
unseen PrimeVul using (2) the search model $`M_{s}`$ and (3) a different
transfer model $`M_{t}`$. PrimeVul provides no optimization feedback.

MetaVul separates harness discovery from evaluation on unseen data and
models. Beginning with a seed harness ($`h_{0}`$), the optimizer
($`\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{opt}}`$) proposes a new harness, using
_validation feedback_. The isolated detector
($`\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{det}}`$) evaluates each harness candidate. After
discovery, MetaVul retains the Pareto-optimal harnesses and evaluates
them on held-out PrimeVul using the search and transfer models.
Fig. [1](#S3.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ MetaVul: Agentic Harness Discovery for Vulnerability Detection")
presents the full pipeline, and
Algorithm [3](#S3 "3 Methodology ‣ MetaVul: Agentic Harness Discovery for Vulnerability Detection")
details the discovery loop.

Table 1: Datasets used by MetaVul. A circled number corresponds to its
respective pipeline stage in
Fig. [1](#S3.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ MetaVul: Agentic Harness Discovery for Vulnerability Detection").

Harness discovery and selection. MetaVul iteratively generates and
evaluates candidate harnesses before selecting those that best balance
its evaluation objectives. Discovery loop. MetaVul first evaluates the
seed harness $`h_{0}`$. At each iteration $`t`$, the optimizer uses
previous harnesses and results to propose $`h_{t}`$, which the detector
evaluates on $`D`$. The results are added to the search history.
Discovery ends after $`T`$ iterations or $`K`$ iterations without
improving pairwise accuracy. Agent roles. The optimizer
$`\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{opt}}`$ revises the harness using validation
feedback. The detector $`\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{det}}`$ runs the proposed
harness and returns predictions for scoring. The agents may use the same
model, but they run separately and never share state. Pareto selection.
After the loop, MetaVul returns the Pareto frontier of all evaluated
harnesses over two validation objectives, pairwise accuracy and joint
hit rate
(Sec. [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Metrics ‣ 4 Experimental Design ‣ MetaVul: Agentic Harness Discovery for Vulnerability Detection")),
both maximized (ParetoFront in
Algorithm [3](#S3 "3 Methodology ‣ MetaVul: Agentic Harness Discovery for Vulnerability Detection")).
Supp. [S6](https://github.com/ARiSE-Lab/MetaVul/blob/main/supplementary_materials/S6_additional_results.pdf)
gives a worked example. We say harness A _dominates_ harness B if A
scores no lower than B on both pairwise accuracy and joint hit rate, and
higher than B on at least one of those metrics. The frontier
$`\mathcal{F}`$ contains those harnesses which are not dominated by any
other harness. If two or more harnesses have identical scores on both
metrics, we keep only the earliest one.

Sandboxing. It is essential that the held-out set is never exposed to
the agent during discovery (the “optimization” phase); otherwise,
contamination would make any held-out gains indistinguishable from
memorization. Neither discovery nor evaluation should be influenced by
system files, default instruction files (such as CLAUDE.md) or user
settings. To address this, we sandbox every agent. The optimizer and
detector agents each run isolated CLI processes that can neither request
nor receive any additional permissions. Each agent is limited in the
data that it can access. As shown in
Fig. [1](#S3.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ MetaVul: Agentic Harness Discovery for Vulnerability Detection"),
the agent and its model serve two roles: an optimizer and a detector
(which we also call the evaluator). Optimizer. The optimizer can only
access its workspace, which holds the validation history: earlier
harnesses, their metrics, and their predictions with labels. After each
iteration, its results are added to the workspace of the next iteration.
Supp. [S10](https://github.com/ARiSE-Lab/MetaVul/blob/main/supplementary_materials/S10_context_budget.pdf)
describes the context budget. For Claude Code, the working directory is
set to the workspace, the read tool is restricted to it, write and edit
tools are denied, and shell access is limited to read-only commands. No
CLAUDE.md files, settings, or memory related to the user or project are
loaded into the context. For Codex, an OS-level sandbox grants read-only
access to the workspace, with no write or network access. Detector. The
detector is launched freshly for every function. To ensure a
non-contaminated run, it has no workspace access (i.e., from the
optimizer), no labels, no trajectory, and no memory between calls. The
detector receives only the rendered harness and one function. For this
phase, Claude Code runs from a /tmp directory with no tools and an empty
system prompt. Similarly, Codex runs the harness in an empty temporary
directory tree with read-only access and no network connection. The
predictions from the held-out PrimeVul evaluation and the cross-model
transfer are never added to any workspace (only the harness changes
between iterations). Detailed agent restrictions are given in
Supp. [S8](https://github.com/ARiSE-Lab/MetaVul/blob/main/supplementary_materials/S8_agent_sandboxing.pdf).

## 4 Experimental Design

We outline our experimental setup: the datasets, seed harness, agents,
models, and configurations
(Sec. [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Datasets, Model, and Agent Selection ‣ 4 Experimental Design ‣ MetaVul: Agentic Harness Discovery for Vulnerability Detection")),
and the evaluation metrics
(Sec. [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Metrics ‣ 4 Experimental Design ‣ MetaVul: Agentic Harness Discovery for Vulnerability Detection")).

### 4.1 Datasets, Model, and Agent Selection

Datasets. We use separate datasets for optimization and testing, so that
we can measure how harness improvements carry over to an unseen dataset
and to models that took no part in optimization. Every sample is a
vulnerable function paired with its patched version.
Table [3](#S3 "3 Methodology ‣ MetaVul: Agentic Harness Discovery for Vulnerability Detection")
summarizes both splits.

- •
  Validation set $`D`$. We handcraft a dataset $`D`$ from TitanVul and
  CWEval. TitanVul ([Li et al., 2026b](#bib.bib14)) combines seven
  public vulnerability datasets and removes duplicate samples. Multiple
  LLM agents check fixes, keeping those that address genuine
  vulnerabilities understandable from the function alone. These checks
  reduce incorrect labels and unrelated code changes. We select 150
  C/C++ pairs, sampled by CWE in proportion to the CWE’s frequency
  (Supp. [S1](https://github.com/ARiSE-Lab/MetaVul/blob/main/supplementary_materials/S1_validation_set.pdf)).
  We enforce some strict criteria, such as ensuring each CWE receives a
  proportional share to its TitanVul occurrence, there is a minimum of
  one of every CWE, even if rare, and pairs with unlabeled CWEs are also
  considered. CWEval ([Peng et al., 2025](#bib.bib26)) evaluates both
  the functional correctness and the security of LLM-generated code;
  each of its security-critical tasks has functional and security tests
  and a secure and an insecure reference implementation. We use all 52
  of its C and C++ tasks, pairing each insecure implementation with its
  secure one. Together these form $`D`$: 202 pairs (404 functions).
  Because 79 of the 150 TitanVul pairs have no CWE label, CWE accuracy
  on $`D`$ is computed over the remaining pairs which do.
- •
  Held-out set. PrimeVul ([Ding et al., 2024](#bib.bib5)) addresses
  several issues of earlier datasets, including noisy labels and
  duplicate functions. PrimeVul contains vulnerable functions and their
  fixes from real open-source C/C++ projects, and we use its paired test
  set as our held-out “unseen” set, as this is a hard benchmark on which
  LLMs reach low pairwise accuracy. Because TitanVul aggregates public
  vulnerability datasets, we checked it for overlap with $`D`$: 5
  PrimeVul pairs contain the same functions and fixes as TitanVul pairs
  in $`D`$. We remove them, leaving 430 pairs (860 functions) from 141
  projects. Each vulnerable function in PrimeVul has a CWE label. The
  optimizer never sees PrimeVul data.

Seed harness. The harness is a standalone Python file that prepares a
function for the detection agent and parses the agent’s verdict. Every
run begins with the same 151-line SCoT seed harness ([Li et al.,
2023](#bib.bib13)), provided in
Supp. [S3](https://github.com/ARiSE-Lab/MetaVul/blob/main/supplementary_materials/S3_seed_harness.pdf).²²
2 In [preliminary
experiments](https://github.com/ARiSE-Lab/MetaVul/blob/main/results/prelim-scot.md),
SCoT achieved higher accuracy and precision than a plain instruction,
MoT, and ToT. Its structure also supports reasoning about sequences,
branches, loops, and patch effects.

Agent selection. We use Codex CLI and Claude Code. In each discovery
session, the optimizer $`\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{opt}}`$ and detector
$`\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{det}}`$ run the same CLI agent and model (only
their access differs). The optimizer can read earlier harnesses,
metrics, and labeled predictions in its workspace. The detector sees
only the harness and one function
(Sec. [3](#S3 "3 Methodology ‣ MetaVul: Agentic Harness Discovery for Vulnerability Detection")).
For unseen-dataset and cross-model transfer, only the detector
($`\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{det}}`$) runs, using the frozen harnesses to
evaluate PrimeVul.

Model selection. We optimized harnesses with Inkling-Small ([Thinking
Machines Lab, 2026](#bib.bib31)), DeepSeek V4 Flash ([OpenRouter,
2026a](#bib.bib19)), Opus 4.6 and GLM-5.3 ([OpenRouter,
2026b](#bib.bib20)). We tested cross-model transfer on Opus 5, Nemotron
3.5 Lightning ([Thinking Machines Lab, 2026](#bib.bib31); [OpenRouter,
2026f](#bib.bib24)), GPT-4o ([OpenRouter, 2026d](#bib.bib22)), GLM-4.7
Flash ([OpenRouter, 2026c](#bib.bib21)) and GPT-OSS-120B ([OpenRouter,
2026e](#bib.bib23)). These models cover smaller and frontier models,
including open-weight and closed models. Opus 4.6 ran through our Claude
subscription, whose usage limits every optimizer and detector call draws
on, so we chose the remaining models from per-token providers
(OpenRouter and Tinker;
Supp. [S12](https://github.com/ARiSE-Lab/MetaVul/blob/main/supplementary_materials/S12_inference_prices.pdf)).

Configurations. Opus 4.6 and Opus 5 ran through our Claude Code
subscription, while all other models were applied through a local
LiteLLM proxy to our external model providers (OpenRouter or Tinker).
All runs allow up to 15 refinement iterations. Inkling-Small and
DeepSeek V4 Flash ran all 15; GLM-5.3 used a patience of 4 and stopped
after iteration 8; Opus 4.6 ran four, limited by subscription usage.
Additional serving, timeout, and decoding configurations are outlined in
Supp. [S9](https://github.com/ARiSE-Lab/MetaVul/blob/main/supplementary_materials/S9_run_configurations.pdf).

### 4.2 Metrics

We evaluate each harness on its detection, discrimination, and
localization ability. Traditional detection metrics. We treat each
function as a binary decision with vulnerable as the positive class, and
report accuracy, precision, recall and F1 over all functions. Pairwise
accuracy. Let pair $`i`$ contain a vulnerable function $`x_{i}^{v}`$ and
its patched version $`x_{i}^{p}`$. For a binary detector $`f`$, pairwise
accuracy over $`N`$ pairs is
$`\operatorname{PairAcc}(f)=\tfrac{1}{N}\sum\nolimits_{i=1}^{N}\mathbf{1}[f(x_{i}^{v})=1\land f(x_{i}^{p})=0]`$.
A pair counts only when both decisions are correct, which makes the
metric stricter than ordinary accuracy.³³ 3 A detector that labels both
the vulnerable function and its patch as vulnerable gets 50% accuracy
and full recall, but $`\mathrm{pAcc}=0`$. Hence, pAcc evaluates the
extent to which the detector is able to identify the fix.
Supp. [S4](https://github.com/ARiSE-Lab/MetaVul/blob/main/supplementary_materials/S4_pairwise_accuracy_example.pdf)
gives a worked example with three detectors. Pairwise accuracy is the
target metric used in
Algorithm [3](#S3 "3 Methodology ‣ MetaVul: Agentic Harness Discovery for Vulnerability Detection").
CWE and localization metrics. These score only true positives, the
vulnerable functions $`i`$ that the harness flags, and only those with
the relevant ground truth: a set of CWEs $`C_{i}`$ (usually one,
sometimes several) and the gold lines $`G_{i}`$. None of the three
datasets marks which lines are vulnerable, so we derive $`G_{i}`$ from
each pair: it contains the lines of the vulnerable function that are
modified or deleted by the fix, or the lines around the insertion point
if the fix only adds lines.⁴⁴ 4 The datasets pair vulnerable code with a
benign associated counterpart. We make use of the lines changed by the
fix as the closest approximation of the vulnerability position. For
CWEval, the fix is the secure reference implementation. For each such
function, the harness returns an ordered list of CWE guesses, whose
first guess is $`\hat{c}_{i}^{(1)}`$, and a set of evidence lines
$`\hat{G}_{i}`$. CWE accuracy is the percentage whose CWE list contains
a CWE in $`C_{i}`$. Loc F1 is the harmonic mean of line-level precision
$`|\hat{G}_{i}\cap G_{i}|/|\hat{G}_{i}|`$ and recall
$`|\hat{G}_{i}\cap G_{i}|/|G_{i}|`$, each averaged over functions, and
loc hit rate is the percentage with at least one correct line
($`\hat{G}_{i}\cap G_{i}\neq\emptyset`$). Joint hit rate. Joint (Joint
in
Algorithm [3](#S3 "3 Methodology ‣ MetaVul: Agentic Harness Discovery for Vulnerability Detection"))
asks whether a correctly flagged function is also explained correctly:
the right vulnerability class in the right place. Let $`T`$ be the set
of flagged vulnerable functions that have both $`C_{i}`$ and $`G_{i}`$.
Function $`i`$ counts as correct only when its first CWE guess is in
$`C_{i}`$ and it has at least one correct line:
$`\operatorname{Joint}=\tfrac{1}{|T|}\sum\nolimits_{i\in T}\mathbf{1}[\hat{c}_{i}^{(1)}\in C_{i}]\cdot\mathbf{1}[\hat{G}_{i}\cap G_{i}\neq\emptyset]`$.
Only the first CWE guess is scored, so a harness cannot earn credit by
listing several candidate CWEs. Regarding parse failures, a function
without a parseable verdict is counted as incorrect and stays in the
denominator for all metrics, so every PrimeVul result covers all
pairs.⁵⁵ 5 Errors from a parse failure are rare, occurring at 0.36%
throughout and at most 0.63% on any individual run.

Motivation & Approach. We ask whether a feedback-driven design can
improve vulnerability-detection harnesses over a starter seed. We
consider metrics such as pairwise accuracy and localization accuracy, as
a strong harness should both tell vulnerable code apart from its fix and
be able to locate the flaw. However, as mentioned, a harness must
balance multiple objectives at once, and a gain on one metric may result
in degradation on another, affecting how the best harness is selected.
We therefore explore whether our approach improves pairwise accuracy and
how these improvements affect other metrics, such as localization. Gains
attained on the data used for optimization could still reflect
overfitting: the harness search could learn task-specific shortcuts that
work on the _validation set_ but disappear on the held-out tasks, or the
harness can overfit to the model that wrote it, performing well on the
model used for optimization but not transferring to other models ([Wang
et al., 2026](#bib.bib35); [Wu et al., 2026](#bib.bib39)). This
motivates RQ1: _Does feedback-driven search improve
vulnerability-detection harnesses, and do the gains transfer to unseen
data and models?_ We conduct four optimization runs using Codex CLI and
Claude Code with Inkling-Small, DeepSeek V4 Flash, Opus 4.6, and
GLM-5.3. Each run begins with the same SCoT seed harness, which we
optimize on validation set $`D`$ using
Algorithm [3](#S3 "3 Methodology ‣ MetaVul: Agentic Harness Discovery for Vulnerability Detection").
At each iteration, we measure pairwise accuracy, precision, recall, CWE
identification, and localization
(Fig. [6](#footnote6 "footnote 6 ‣ Figure 2 ‣ 5 Discovery and Transfer ‣ MetaVul: Agentic Harness Discovery for Vulnerability Detection")).
To determine the Pareto frontier, we use pairwise accuracy and joint hit
rate on the validation set. Then, without changing the harnesses, we
evaluate each of the harnesses on PrimeVul: first with the model used
for optimization, then with a model not used during optimization. These
transfer models are Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, GLM-4.7 Flash, Opus 5, and
GPT-OSS-120B
(Fig. [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5 Discovery and Transfer ‣ MetaVul: Agentic Harness Discovery for Vulnerability Detection")).⁷⁷
7
Supp. [S6](https://github.com/ARiSE-Lab/MetaVul/blob/main/supplementary_materials/S6_additional_results.pdf)
shows each column at full width and gives a worked example of selecting
the Pareto frontier. For each evaluation, we report the best harness
from the validation frontier.
Supp. [S5](https://github.com/ARiSE-Lab/MetaVul/blob/main/supplementary_materials/S5_rq1_full_metrics.pdf)
reports every metric for the seed and best harness, shows how pairwise
accuracy correlates with the other metrics, and shows how many harnesses
beat the seed on each metric.

Results. Feedback-driven optimization improves validation pairwise
accuracy in all four runs, with best-harness gains over the seed of
$`+`$21.3 (Inkling-Small), $`+`$21.8 (DeepSeek V4 Flash), $`+`$23.3
(Opus 4.6) and $`+`$11.4 points (GLM-5.3)
(Fig. [6](#footnote6 "footnote 6 ‣ Figure 2 ‣ 5 Discovery and Transfer ‣ MetaVul: Agentic Harness Discovery for Vulnerability Detection")),
and all 40 discovered harnesses beat the seed. The gains largely carry
over: a frontier harness beats the seed in all 8 held-out and
cross-model evaluations
(Fig. [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5 Discovery and Transfer ‣ MetaVul: Agentic Harness Discovery for Vulnerability Detection")).
On unseen PrimeVul data with the same model, the gains are $`+`$11.9,
$`+`$25.8, $`+`$8.4 and $`+`$5.6 points in the same order; on models
that took no part in optimization, they are $`+`$8.4 on Nemotron 3.5
Lightning, $`+`$7.9 on GLM-4.7 Flash, $`+`$14.7 on Opus 5 and $`+`$4.7
on GPT-OSS-120B. Pairwise accuracy generally increases with precision
while recall decreases. Its relationship with joint hit rate differs
across models, indicating a negative association for Inkling-Small and
DeepSeek V4 Flash and a positive association for GLM-5.3
(Supp. Table [S5.2](https://github.com/ARiSE-Lab/MetaVul/blob/main/supplementary_materials/S5_rq1_full_metrics.pdf)).
Only 10 of the 40 harnesses improve localization
(Supp. Table [S5.3](https://github.com/ARiSE-Lab/MetaVul/blob/main/supplementary_materials/S5_rq1_full_metrics.pdf)).
Consequently, these implications motivate the application of a Pareto
frontier, rather than one specific harness chosen strictly on one of the
criteria provided.

## 6 Comparison to Other Methods

Motivation & Approach. Related work evaluates four LLM-based and agentic
vulnerability detectors on PrimeVul using GPT-4o, providing a common
backbone for comparison
(Sec. [2](#S2 "2 Related Work ‣ MetaVul: Agentic Harness Discovery for Vulnerability Detection")).
This motivates RQ2: _How does MetaVul compare with other LLM-based or
agentic methods?_ Because GPT-4o was costly to evaluate through
OpenRouter, our budget did not permit transferring every discovered
harness. We randomly selected the DeepSeek V4 Flash discovery run and
evaluated the six harnesses with the highest validation pairwise
accuracy to test whether its strongest candidates transferred to
GPT-4o.⁸⁸ 8 At the time of evaluation, GPT-4o cost \$10 per million
output tokens on OpenRouter. We also evaluated iteration 7; iteration 13
did not complete.
Supp. [S7](https://github.com/ARiSE-Lab/MetaVul/blob/main/supplementary_materials/S7_gpt4o_transfer.pdf)
reports all completed transfers, while
Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5 Discovery and Transfer ‣ MetaVul: Agentic Harness Discovery for Vulnerability Detection")
compares the seed with iteration 12, the transferred harness with the
highest accuracy.

Results. MetaVul correctly discriminates 103 of 435 pairs, compared with
74 for the seed and 81 for the next-best method, whose results are
reported from prior work
(Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5 Discovery and Transfer ‣ MetaVul: Agentic Harness Discovery for Vulnerability Detection")).
Notably, MetaVul uses a single detector agent, whereas GPTLens, VulTrial
and ConfColl coordinate multiple agents. After removing 5 pairs
overlapping validation, MetaVul still correctly discriminates 100 of 430
pairs. It also achieves the highest accuracy and the lowest
false-positive rate among methods with non-trivial recall. The GPT-4o
evaluation was limited to a subset of discovered harnesses due to budget
constraints. This result should not be considered an upper bound. The
evaluation of additional harnesses may in fact yield stronger
performance results.

## 7 Optimization Integrity

Motivation & Approach. Because the optimizer receives labeled validation
feedback, its gains could come from shortcuts rather than better harness
design. We therefore ask RQ3: _Do MetaVul’s gains rely on data leakage,
embedded answers, or trivial verdict bias?_ We test two possible
shortcut pathways. First, we verify that the optimizer cannot access
PrimeVul during discovery. Second, we use GPT-OSS-120B as a judge to
examine all 44 harnesses using only their text. The judge assigns
numerical ratings from 0 to 4 (where 0 means missing/unusable and 4
means precise/complete) for respecting relevant constraints: (1) for
preserving SCoT, (2) for avoiding prohibited content such as examples,
labels, dataset hints, or verdict-bias instructions, and (3) for
preserving the output format.
Table [3](#S7.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 7 Optimization Integrity ‣ MetaVul: Agentic Harness Discovery for Vulnerability Detection")
reports these checks for the Pareto-frontier harnesses, with full judge
results in
Supp. [S2](https://github.com/ARiSE-Lab/MetaVul/blob/main/supplementary_materials/S2_harness_quality.pdf).

|                           |                     |       |               |        |              |                   |
| ------------------------- | ------------------- | ----- | ------------- | ------ | ------------ | ----------------- |
| Agent + Model             | Frontier iterations | SCoT  | No prohibited | Output | FP reduction | Flagged reduction |
| Codex + Inkling-Small     | 6, 8, 12            | 3/3   | 3/3           | 3/3    | 33-44%       | 31-36%            |
| Codex + DeepSeek V4 Flash | 1, 5, 9, 11, 14     | 5/5   | 5/5           | 4/5    | 44-60%       | 34-49%            |
| Claude Code + Opus 4.6    | 2, 3                | 2/2   | 2/2           | 2/2    | 50%          | 35-37%            |
| Claude Code + GLM-5.3     | 6                   | 1/1   | 1/1           | 0/1    | 49%          | 35%               |
| Total                     | 11 harnesses        | 11/11 | 11/11         | 9/11   | 33-60%       | 31-49%            |

Table 3: Shortcut checks for Pareto-frontier harnesses. The ratings
indicate how many of the frontier harnesses receive a $`4/4`$ score for
preserving SCoT, avoiding prohibited content, and preserving the output
format. The final columns show how much the frontier harnesses cut FP
(false positives) and total flagged “vulnerable” functions, compared to
the run’s seed.
Supp. [S2](https://github.com/ARiSE-Lab/MetaVul/blob/main/supplementary_materials/S2_harness_quality.pdf)
shows more detailed results.

Results. We find no evidence that the Pareto-frontier harnesses exploit
the tested shortcuts. All 11 receive $`4/4`$ for preserving SCoT and
avoiding prohibited content. Two receive lower output-format ratings
because of conflicting instructions, a quality issue rather than a
shortcut. Every frontier harness reduces both false positives and the
total number of flagged functions, with false positives falling by 33%
to 60%.

## 8 Limitations

We identify some limitations and threats in this work. Same model for
both roles. During harness discovery, the detection agent and the
optimizer agent use the same model. Our cross-model transfer experiments
help to mitigate this risk. We tested whether the discovered harnesses
still improved detection rates on models that took _no_ part in
optimization, and showed that the gains carry over, hence the gains
cannot be attributed to one specific model. Seed harness. Although we
selected a strong seed based on a pilot comparison of different
reasoning strategies, ultimately, the space of possible seeds is large,
so it was infeasible to test whether other seeds lead to different or
better harnesses. Contribution of workspace components. We do not
establish which parts of the optimizer’s workspace (earlier harnesses,
aggregate metrics, the score history, or example-by-example predictions
with labels) account for the improvement. A preliminary ablation that
removed these components level by level was inconclusive
(Supp. [S11](https://github.com/ARiSE-Lab/MetaVul/blob/main/supplementary_materials/S11_ablation.pdf)).
Language and granularity. All experiments operate on C/C++ functions, so
results may not carry over to memory-safe or dynamically typed
languages. Detection is also performed at the function level, without
any surrounding context or access to the rest of the repository. Cost
and access to infrastructure. Access to API infrastructure was a severe
limitation, although the results so far are very promising. Because both
agents are launched as CLI processes (codex exec and claude -p), we
mostly relied on subscriptions rather than per-token API billing to
obtain these results. Subscriptions are limited by 5-hour and weekly
usage windows, and a single optimization run, which evaluates every
candidate harness on 404 functions, exhausts them very quickly.
OpenRouter options for open-weight models were cheap (for example,
\$0.03 per million input tokens and \$0.17 per million output tokens for
GPT-OSS-120B;
Supp. [S12](https://github.com/ARiSE-Lab/MetaVul/blob/main/supplementary_materials/S12_inference_prices.pdf)),
but GPT-4o was not, at \$2.50 per million input tokens and \$10.00 per
million output tokens ([OpenRouter, 2026d](#bib.bib22)). Due to these
previously listed constraints, we were limited by the number of feasible
iterations, repeated runs, and model pairings. Data contamination. We
cannot fully exclude that the benchmarks appeared in the models’
training data. Some of the evaluated models have training cutoffs that
postdate the release of the benchmarks available. However, the three
following observations directly suggest that this is unlikely and
mitigate this concern. GPT-4o has a training cutoff (October 2023) that
precedes the release of PrimeVul, TitanVul and CWEval, and harnesses
learned with DeepSeek V4 Flash still improve on it (79-101 vs. 71
correct pairs;
Supp. [S7](https://github.com/ARiSE-Lab/MetaVul/blob/main/supplementary_materials/S7_gpt4o_transfer.pdf)).
The seed harness also scores near the floor on pairwise accuracy
($`10.5\%`$), which memorized fixes would not produce, and grouping all
430 PrimeVul pairs by CVE year (2008-2022) shows no monotonic trend.⁹⁹ 9
We maintain that, if a model memorized fixes during training, older
bugs, which have been public for longer, should be easier. Each PrimeVul
pair is a real bug reported in a particular year. So, to test this, we
group pairs by year (2008-2022) and measure performance in each group.
We found no consistent trend across runs. Per-year results are in our
[CVE-year
report](https://github.com/ARiSE-Lab/MetaVul/blob/main/results/cve_year/report.md).

## 9 Future Work

There are several directions that could be targeted by future work.
First, it could be worthwhile to swap or pair different optimizer and
detector agents, for example a smaller detector with a stronger
optimizer, or Claude Code with Codex, to measure how much each role
contributes to the discovered harnesses. The trade-off between
discrimination, localization, and CWE identification should also be
studied directly, since techniques that improve these metrics together
remain underexplored. Starting discovery from a different seed harness
could also show how the seed limits or biases evolution downstream. We
can also think of many enhancements to the harness itself, such as a
spec-driven approach to harness design, where a declarative
specification can outline the input and output format, constrain each
candidate harness, and check it before evaluation. The detector could
also be given other context, like pre-extracted data-flow and program
dependence graphs, or call graphs and caller/callee information (using
the whole project), which can be pre-computed for the data and included
in the workspace. Finally, direct integration into agentic exploit
generation could be explored, which has implications for improving cost
and efficiency.

## 10 Conclusion

MetaVul automatically discovers vulnerability-detection harnesses that
outperform a hand-designed seed. Across four runs, validation pairwise
accuracy improves by 11.4-23.3 points ($`1.6\times`$-$`4.3\times`$).
These gains persist across all eight held-out and cross-model
evaluations (up to 25.8 points on unseen PrimeVul data and 14.7 on an
unseen model). On GPT-4o, a transferred harness correctly discriminates
103 of 435 pairs, outperforming existing methods and achieving the
highest accuracy. We find no evidence of shortcuts: every
Pareto-frontier harness preserves SCoT, avoids prohibited content, and
reduces false positives by 33%-60%. MetaVul thus addresses two
challenges. Firstly, it _reduces false alarms_, cutting false positives
while improving discrimination between security-relevant changes and
benign code variations. Secondly, it _improves generalization_, showing
that the gains hold on unseen data and unseen models rather than
overfitting.

These results have further implications for real-world vulnerability
detection, including, but not limited to, analyzing new codebases,
automated exploit generation, and triage. First, the transferability
results show that this technique can transfer to unseen codebases.
Second, it can make automated exploit generation more efficient and
scalable: it can filter out benign code from promising vulnerabilities
before exploit generation and execution, which are computationally
expensive (see Future Work,
Sec. [9](#S9 "9 Future Work ‣ MetaVul: Agentic Harness Discovery for Vulnerability Detection")).
Even after exploit generation, people must decide how serious an exploit
is, what its potential downstream effects are, and how quickly a fix
should be applied. Thus, there are major implications for security
auditing and triage, as this technique can reduce the need for developer
intervention.

## Reproducibility Statement

Our code has been publicly available at
[https://github.com/ARiSE-Lab/MetaVul](https://github.com/ARiSE-Lab/MetaVul) ([ARiSE
Lab, 2026](#bib.bib2)) since September 30, 2026. This work, from
conception to implementation, took place between February and September 2026.

## Acknowledgements

Part of this work was supported by a Tinker Grant from Thinking Machines
Lab (TML). We thank TML for their support. We also thank Ciaran
Ramasastry Walsh for his discussions and early explorations in the Codex
environment.

## AI Use Statement

We used AI to improve transitions and wording in our writing to make it
clearer for our audience in cases where page limit constraints are a
concern. We used our hand-written drafts prior to improving transitions
or wording. We did not use AI to conceive any research ideas. All ideas
came from reading the literature and related work, discussions among the
authors, and insights from past projects, and we first wrote our own
notes and human-authored drafts. We also used Claude Code and Codex for
code maintenance and debugging. All AI-assisted text and code were
reviewed by the authors.
